question: Every model class exposes a manager that the ORM itself uses when it must query a table without any user-supplied filtering, and the attribute reachable on the model class is only a one-line property on the metaclass that forwards to the Meta options object. On the options object the value is computed and cached, and it is that computation that holds the real policy: when the model's Meta does not name one, it walks the MRO and adopts the name used by the first ancestor whose own such manager is not the fabricated default; if a name is configured but no manager with that name is registered on the model it raises ValueError naming the object and the missing name; and when no name can be determined it builds a fresh plain Manager, assigns it a reserved underscore-prefixed name, binds it to the model and flags it as automatically created. Which definition performs that computation? Return the qualified symbol as path::name.
author_notes: Trap (clause 1): a search for the internal manager lands first on ModelBase._base_manager in django/db/models/base.py, which is a two-line property whose whole body is `return cls._meta.base_manager`; a system that stops at the first plausible symbol answers base.py and is wrong. Proof: Options.base_manager (options.py, @cached_property) contains the MRO walk that reads `parent._base_manager.name != "_base_manager"`, the `managers_map[base_manager_name]` lookup wrapped in the ValueError with the "%s has no manager named %r" message, and the final fabrication path that sets `manager.name = "_base_manager"`, `manager.model = self.model` and `manager.auto_created = True`. Clause 5: the lookup step is only correct because Options.managers_map is itself derived from Options.managers, which copies each local manager, dedupes by name and sorts by (mro depth, creation counter) — so the described error only fires for names absent from that merged map, not merely absent from Meta. Clause 2: answering requires combining the metaclass property, the cached property, and the managers/managers_map pair. Alternates: base.py::_base_manager is the forwarding property, not the policy; options.py::default_manager is the parallel namesake with different fallback rules (it consults local_managers and returns managers[0], never fabricating one); managers_map and managers build the registry consumed by the answer; ManagerDescriptor.__get__ in manager.py resolves an instance-level access through managers_map and raises for abstract/swapped models, which is a third distinct code path.

question: django/db/models contains two definitions that share one name and mean very different things. One of them is a query builder used while a cascade is being planned: it receives a model on the far side of a set of relation fields plus one batch of already-collected instances, composes a single predicate by OR-connecting one `<field name>__in` term per relation field through Q.create, and returns a queryset taken from the far model's internal unfiltered manager pinned to the alias the planner is deleting on. The other definition of the same name is pure field metadata and performs no database access at all. Identify the query-builder one and return it as path::name.
author_notes: Clause 4: `related_objects` is defined twice inside django/db/models — as Collector.related_objects in deletion.py and as the Options cached property in options.py — so a leaf-name answer is ambiguous and the question demands a path. Clause 1: the first hit for anything phrased around a model's related objects is the Options cached property, which returns an ImmutableList built from `_get_fields(forward=False, reverse=True, include_hidden=True)` and issues no query; the described behaviour (Q.create with connector=Q.OR, `_base_manager.using(self.using).filter(predicate)`) only exists in deletion.py. Clause 5: the deletion.py definition is only correct in light of its caller — Collector.collect splits `new_objs` with get_del_batches and passes one batch at a time as `objs`, and it passes either a single field or the accumulated `related_fields` list for the fast-delete case, which is why the method must OR the terms rather than AND them; its use of the internal unfiltered manager (not the default manager) is what makes the cascade see rows a custom manager would hide. Alternates: options.py::related_objects is the metadata namesake and the designed trap; get_del_batches produces the batches the answer consumes; collect is the caller; _populate_directed_relation_graph builds the reverse-relation graph feeding the metadata namesake.

question: The model base class defines a method that guards against silent data loss from unsaved related objects. It walks the model's concrete fields, optionally restricted to a subset of fields handed to it, and for every relation whose value is already cached on the instance it inspects the target: if the target has no primary key it evicts the reverse cache entry when the relation is not multiple and raises ValueError whose message is prefixed by the name of the operation it was told it is serving; if the target was saved after being assigned it re-assigns it so the key is copied over; and if the target's key no longer matches the stored value it drops the stale cached relation. It then repeats the unsaved-target check over the private fields that carry a separate key field. List every function or method in the corpus, outside the module that defines that guard, which calls it. Return each as path::name.

evidence.contains: "%s() prohibited to prevent data loss due to unsaved "

author_notes: Proof: ripgrep for `_prepare_related_fields_for_save(` finds exactly three call sites. base.py:848 is inside Model.save and lives in the guard's own module, so it is excluded. The two remaining ones are query.py:701, which sits inside the private per-object preparer QuerySet._prepare_for_bulk_create (it passes operation_name="bulk_create"), and query.py:894, inside QuerySet.bulk_update (it passes operation_name="bulk_update" plus the resolved `fields` list). Two enclosing definitions, hence exhaustive=true. Clause 1: the first plausible symbol is QuerySet.bulk_create, and the string "bulk_create" literally appears at the call site — but bulk_create does not call the guard; it delegates to _prepare_for_bulk_create, so a system that maps the call-site keyword argument or the obvious public entry point to a caller answers bulk_create and is wrong. The other obvious caller, Model.save, is in the excluded module. Clause 5: the guard's contract is only readable through its callers — `operation_name` is purely a message prefix supplied by each caller, and the `fields=` restriction is exercised by exactly one of the two (the batched field-update path, which must skip fields outside the update list), so neither the parameter list nor the raise text can be understood from the definition alone. Clause 3: reaching the answer needs the call-site line resolved to its enclosing private preparer rather than to the public method above it. Alternates: bulk_create is the designed trap; save and save_base are same-module (save_base does not call it at all, it is one frame below save); _save_table performs the UPDATE/INSERT split and never touches related caches; _batched_insert receives the already-prepared objects.

question: In the Meta options layer there is a method used when building joins for multi-table inheritance: given a candidate ancestor model it returns the field on the current model that points at that ancestor, recursing through the immediate parents when the link is indirect, and for a proxied model returning the first link of the chain in preference to the recursively found one; it returns None when the given model is not an ancestor at all. Identify that method, and also identify every function or method in the corpus outside the module that defines it which calls it. Answer as a JSON object with keys "implementation" and "callers", where the implementation is one path::name and callers is a list of path::name.
author_notes: Proof: the described recursion with the proxy-aware `return self.parents[parent] or parent_link` is unique to Options.get_ancestor_link. Ripgrep for the name finds six use sites: two inside options.py itself (get_path_from_parent and the method's own recursive call), which the name-based caller check excludes as same-module, and exactly four elsewhere — DeferredAttribute._check_parent_chain in query_utils.py, Query.join_parent_model in sql/query.py, ForeignObject.get_instance_value_for_fields in fields/related.py, and ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.__get__ in fields/related_descriptors.py. Four enclosing definitions, hence exhaustive=true. Clause 1: searching for inheritance-join helpers surfaces get_path_to_parent/get_path_from_parent first — both are PathInfo builders that merely consume the answer, so the first plausible symbol is a distractor, and get_path_from_parent's call site is in the same module and must be discarded rather than reported. Clause 3: the caller half spans four modules, one of the callers is a dunder descriptor hook that a name search alone cannot disambiguate without resolving the enclosing class, and the two same-module uses must be filtered out. Clause 5: the answer's contract is only readable through caller and callee — it recurses into `parent._meta` of itself for indirect links, and _check_parent_chain is only sound because the returned link is compared against `self.field` before `getattr(instance, link_field.attname)` is used, i.e. the deferred-loading shortcut depends on the answer returning the pointer field rather than the primary key itself. Alternates: get_path_to_parent and get_path_from_parent are consumers (the latter's call site is inside the defining module); get_base_chain returns the model chain the path builders iterate, not a field; all_parents is the parent set, not the link; query_utils.py::__get__ is the neighbouring DeferredAttribute hook that delegates to the real caller in that module instead of using the answer directly.

question: When a relation field is added to a model, the Meta options object of the model on the far side of that relation has only one direction of its memoized state invalidated — the direction describing incoming references — while the model receiving the field has everything invalidated. That one-directional invalidation iterates a class-level set of attribute names and deletes each from the instance dictionary, and it is skipped entirely for abstract models. Identify every cached definition in the corpus that this one-directional pass can drop. Return each as path::name.
author_notes: Clause 3: the answer is a three-hop traversal — Options.add_field calls `field.remote_field.model._meta._expire_cache(forward=False)` for a relation field, _expire_cache's reverse branch (`if reverse and not self.abstract`) iterates self.REVERSE_PROPERTIES, and that class attribute names exactly three cached properties, each of which must then be located as a definition in options.py. Clause 2: neither the constant nor any single method answers it; the set of names and the set of @cached_property definitions have to be combined, and the abstract guard has to be read to state the condition correctly. Clause 1: FORWARD_PROPERTIES sits on the immediately preceding lines and holds eleven names (fields, many_to_many, concrete_fields, local_concrete_fields, _non_pk_concrete_field_names, _reverse_one_to_one_field_names, _forward_fields_map, managers, managers_map, base_manager, default_manager); a system that grabs the first constant it sees, or that reads add_field's unconditional `self._expire_cache()` branch instead of the `forward=False` one, returns that larger forward set. Alternates: _forward_fields_map, fields, concrete_fields and managers_map are forward-set members dropped only by a full or forward invalidation; _populate_directed_relation_graph writes `_relation_tree` straight into __dict__ for every model and is the producer, not a droppable cached definition; _expire_cache is the mechanism performing the deletion. Note `_get_fields_cache` is also reset, but it is a plain dict initialised in __init__, not a definition, and is cleared on every invalidation regardless of direction.

question: In the module that defines Django's aggregate function classes, one override of the standard expression-resolution hook behaves unlike every other override of that hook. It forwards the query, join permission, alias reuse and summarize arguments to its superclass but deliberately drops the save-time flag; it raises a field error when a summarized call refers to an annotation that is itself summarized; and when the caller supplied a fallback for the empty-result case, it blanks that fallback on the copy it made and then returns a *different* expression object entirely - a two-argument first-non-null function wrapping that copy together with the fallback, carrying the copy's summary flag - rather than returning the aggregate. Name the path-qualified method that does this.

evidence.contains: # Aggregates are not allowed in UPDATE queries, so ignore for_save
c.default = None  # Reset the default argument before wrapping.
if default is not None and self.empty_result_set_value is not None:

author_notes: Difficulty clauses 2, 4 and 5. Clause 4: the corpus defines this hook name in ten different files (aggregates.py, expressions.py, lookups.py, indexes.py, query.py, query_utils.py, sql/query.py, sql/where.py, fields/related_lookups.py, functions/datetime.py) and several times inside expressions.py alone; only the aggregates.py implementation matches the described behaviour, so the answer must be path-qualified. Clause 2: the described behaviour cannot be read off one definition - the 'blanks the fallback and returns something else' step is only intelligible together with Aggregate.__init__ (which rejects `default` when `empty_result_set_value` is set, so the two mechanisms are mutually exclusive) and with functions/comparison.py::Coalesce, the two-argument first-non-null wrapper that is actually returned. Clause 5: the dropped save-time flag is only correct given what the callee does - the override calls `super().resolve_expression(query, allow_joins, reuse, summarize)` with four positional arguments where the base in expressions.py accepts five, and the comment names the reason (aggregates are illegal in UPDATE). Proof: aggregates.py lines 59-103 - `c = super().resolve_expression(query, allow_joins, reuse, summarize)`, the `FieldError` raised for a summarized ref whose annotation `is_summary`, `c.default = None  # Reset the default argument before wrapping.`, `coalesce = Coalesce(c, default, ...)`, `coalesce.is_summary = c.is_summary`, `return coalesce`. Alternates: expressions.py::resolve_expression is the first hit any search for this hook returns (BaseExpression's copy-and-resolve-sources implementation) but it knows nothing about filters, summaries or fallbacks; sql/query.py::resolve_expression resolves a Query used as an expression and lookups.py::resolve_expression resolves lhs/rhs of a lookup, neither wraps anything; functions/comparison.py::Coalesce is the class of the returned object, not the method asked for - naming it is the classic one-step-short answer; aggregates.py::as_sql is the other distinctive Aggregate override (it handles FILTER/CASE WHEN) and is what a search for 'aggregate' plus 'default' in the same file can surface first.

question: Inside django/db/models/sql, one small module-level function - not a method - interprets a single ORDER BY specification: it is handed a field specification and a default direction, looks that default up in a two-entry table that pairs each direction with its opposite, and returns the field specification stripped of any leading minus sign together with the direction, where a leading minus always means the opposite of the supplied default. Identify that function and every definition outside its own module that calls it directly. Answer with path-qualified symbols.
author_notes: Difficulty clauses 1, 2 and 3. Clause 1: every plausible first hit is a distractor. A search for ordering in the compiler surfaces `get_order_by`, which is the public entry point and contains no call to the helper at all - it consumes the generator; a search for the direction table surfaces constants.py::ORDER_DIR, data rather than the function; `add_ordering` in sql/query.py validates specs with ORDER_PATTERN and again never calls the helper. Clause 3: solving it takes two hops in opposite directions - first identify the helper from its behaviour (sql/query.py, module level, bottom of the file, not a Query method), then enumerate its call sites in a different module, where both live one level below the obvious public method: `_order_by_pairs` (the private generator `get_order_by` iterates) and `find_ordering_name` (recursive, reached from the generator via Meta.ordering expansion). Clause 2: the returned direction is only correct when combined with constants.py::ORDER_DIR - the function itself never spells ASC or DESC, it indexes `dirn[0]`/`dirn[1]` out of the pair, and the caller-supplied default is itself computed from `ORDER_DIR["ASC"]` or `ORDER_DIR["DESC"]` depending on `query.standard_ordering`, so reverse() flips what a leading minus means. Proof: sql/query.py lines 2632-2643 define the function; compiler.py line 377 (`col, order = get_order_dir(field, default_order)`, inside `_order_by_pairs`) and line 1047 (`name, order = get_order_dir(name, default_order)`, inside `find_ordering_name`) are the only call sites outside sql/query.py - an independent name-based enumeration over the whole corpus returns exactly these two, hence `exhaustive`. Alternates: get_order_by and get_distinct are the ordering-adjacent compiler methods a shallow answer names, but neither calls the helper; add_ordering is the Query-side ordering mutator; _setup_joins is the shared helper of get_order_by and get_distinct and is a tempting near-miss because find_ordering_name sits beside it; ORDER_PATTERN is not a definition of the described function.

question: The SQL predicate-tree module defines a method that rewrites table aliases in a node's children in place rather than returning a new tree: handed a mapping from current alias to new alias, it returns immediately when the mapping is empty, recurses into any child that can rewrite aliases itself, and otherwise replaces the child in position with the result of asking that child for an alias-rewritten copy. Which definitions outside that module call this method directly? Answer with path-qualified symbols.

evidence.contains: Relabel the alias values of any children. 'change_map' is a dictionary

author_notes: Difficulty clauses 1, 3 and 5. Clause 1: the first plausible symbol is a distractor that lives in the helper's own module. where.py::relabeled_clone is the immediate textual neighbour, it calls the helper, and it is what a search for alias relabelling returns first - but it is inside the helper's module and is therefore not an outside caller; the same trap exists one layer out, where datastructures.py and expressions.py each define relabeled_clone, the *callee* side of the branch described in the question. Clause 3: two hops - identify the in-place mutator in sql/where.py from its behaviour (empty-map early return, recursion for alias-rewriting children, positional replacement via a rewritten copy otherwise), then find its external call sites, which are both inside sql/query.py and both reached only through alias bookkeeping: `change_aliases` relabels the query's own predicate tree as part of renaming aliases, and `combine` clones the right-hand query's predicate tree and relabels that clone before adding it. Clause 5: the helper is only correct given what its children do - it never rewrites an alias itself, it dispatches on which of two protocols a child implements (`relabel_aliases` in place, or `relabeled_clone` returning a replacement), so reading the method alone does not tell you what happens to a leaf predicate. Proof: where.py lines 203-215 define it; sql/query.py line 757 (`w.relabel_aliases(change_map)` in `combine`) and line 988 (`self.where.relabel_aliases(change_map)` in `change_aliases`) are the only calls outside where.py - an independent name-based enumeration across the corpus returns exactly these two, hence `exhaustive`. Alternates: the three relabeled_clone entries are the callee protocol and the same-module wrapper, never external callers; query.py::bump_prefix renames aliases but delegates to change_aliases and does not call the helper; compiler.py::pre_sql_setup is the ordering/alias-touching compiler hook a keyword search offers and calls neither.

question: The base SQL compiler contains a method that implements grouping reduction by functional dependence. When (and only when) the connection's feature flags report that grouping by selected primary keys is allowed, it computes the set of grouped expressions that are primary-key columns of a model the backend permits this optimisation for, and then keeps an expression only if it is one of those primary-key columns, or if it appears in the method's second argument - the grouping columns its caller extracted from the HAVING clause - or if its alias is not one of the tables whose primary key is already grouped. On any other backend it returns what it was given, unchanged. Name that method, path-qualified.
author_notes: Difficulty clauses 1, 2 and 5. Clause 1: the first plausible symbol is the caller. Any search for GROUP BY construction in the compiler lands on `get_group_by` - the long, heavily commented method whose docstring says the logic is hard to describe - and that method does contain `allows_group_by_select_index` handling and the whole group-by assembly, so a system that stops at the first strong hit answers with the caller rather than with the one-line-lower reduction step. `allows_group_by_selected_pks` and `allows_group_by_select_index` are also easy to confuse: the first belongs to the answer, the second to the caller. Clause 5: the method's second parameter is meaningless on its own - reading the definition alone tells you only that expressions 'in having' survive; what `having` actually is (the result of `self.having.get_group_by_cols()`, an empty tuple when there is no HAVING clause) is established solely at the call site in the caller, which is the definition of a helper whose behaviour is only correct given what its caller passed. Clause 2: the keep/drop rule needs two more definitions to be read correctly - Col.target/alias in expressions.py (the `hasattr(expr, "target")` and `expr.alias` probes only match column references) and the backend feature pair `allows_group_by_selected_pks` / `allows_group_by_selected_pks_on_model`, which excludes unmanaged models. Proof: compiler.py lines 197-227 are the definition, with `pks = {...}`, `aliases = {expr.alias for expr in pks}` and the `expr in pks or expr in having or getattr(expr, "alias", None) not in aliases` filter, plus the unconditional `return expressions` outside the feature branch; line 169 computes `having_group_by` and line 174 passes it in. Alternates: get_group_by is the designed trap (the caller); set_group_by in sql/query.py sets `query.group_by` and does no reduction; the two get_group_by_cols entries are what grouped expressions are *collected* with, not reduced with; get_select is the neighbouring compiler method that produces the select list the caller grouping is derived from.

question: A query object in django/db/models/sql can itself be embedded inside another query, so it implements the same compile-time interface as an ordinary expression. One method on it produces the SQL text and the parameter list for that embedding, and it does three things in order: unless the connection's feature flags say the backend already ignores a redundant ORDER BY inside a subquery, it clears the ordering - without forcing, so an explicitly forced ordering survives - on itself and on every one of its set-operation operands; then it obtains a compiler for the given connection and asks that compiler to produce the statement; then, only when the query is flagged as a subquery, it wraps the produced text in parentheses. Give the path-qualified method.
author_notes: Difficulty clauses 1, 2 and 4. Clause 4: the corpus defines this method name in thirteen files, and in several of them many times over (sql/compiler.py has five, expressions.py more than a dozen, where.py four, lookups.py several) - only the single definition on the Query class in sql/query.py matches the described behaviour, which is why the question demands a path-qualified answer. Clause 1: the natural first hit is a distractor. Searching for subquery compilation surfaces expressions.py::Subquery (whose own implementation formats a template around `query.as_sql`) or the compiler's top-level statement builder, and both are one step away from the method actually described; the parenthesising step in particular looks like something an expression wrapper should own, while here it is the query that does it based on its own `subquery` flag. Clause 2: the behaviour is not readable from one definition. `clear_ordering(force=False, clear_default=True)` in the same module decides what 'without forcing' means - a query whose ordering was forced keeps it - and the `subquery` flag defaults to False on the class, so both the ORDER BY stripping and the parentheses depend on state set elsewhere; the delegation target is a third definition, `get_compiler`, which needs `using` or `connection` and raises otherwise. Proof: sql/query.py lines 1253-1266 - the `self.subquery and not connection.features.ignores_unnecessary_order_by_in_subqueries` guard, `self.clear_ordering(force=False)` followed by the same call over `self.combined_queries`, `sql, params = self.get_compiler(connection=connection).as_sql()`, and `sql = "(%s)" % sql` under `if self.subquery`. Alternates: expressions.py's namesake is the designed trap (Subquery/Exists formatting, no ordering surgery); the compiler namesake builds the SELECT statement itself and is the callee, not the method described; where.py's namesake compiles predicate trees; get_compiler and clear_ordering are the two callees this method combines, each a one-step-short answer.

question: django/db/backends/utils.py defines a module-level helper that folds its string arguments into a single md5 built with usedforsecurity=False and returns a prefix of the hex digest whose length the caller supplies as a keyword argument. Enumerate every function or method defined outside django/db/backends/utils.py that calls that helper directly. Return each as path::name in a JSON list.
author_notes: Difficulty clauses 1, 3 and 5. The helper is names_digest in django/db/backends/utils.py. Clause 1: the very first call site a search returns is the one inside the same file, truncate_name at django/db/backends/utils.py:296 ('digest = names_digest(name, length=hash_len)'). It is the most prominent and most plausible answer, but the question explicitly asks only for callers defined outside that module, so a system that stops at the first hit answers with a symbol that is excluded by construction. Clause 3: the remaining call sites are only two, and both are reached from schema/index name generation, so the tempting continuation is to report the callers of those callers - _create_index_sql and _create_unique_sql invoke _create_index_name, and Options._prepare and ForeignObjectRel-side code in fields/related.py reach the digest only through truncate_name. Those are two hops away and are not direct callers. Clause 5: the helper's behaviour (a short, deterministic, non-security digest used to make identifiers unique within a length budget) is only intelligible from what its two real callers do with it - concatenating table and column names in base/schema.py::_create_index_name and hash_data in indexes.py::set_name_with_model - so the answer cannot be read off the definition alone. Proof: ripgrep for 'names_digest(' across the corpus yields exactly three call sites, one of them inside the defining module; the two remaining enclosing definitions are BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor._create_index_name (django/db/backends/base/schema.py:1495 is inside the method that begins at line 1486) and Index.set_name_with_model (django/db/models/indexes.py:183 is inside the method that begins at line 158). Declared exhaustive on that enumeration. Alternates fail: truncate_name is a genuine caller but lives in the helper's own module, which the question excludes; _create_index_sql and _create_unique_sql call _create_index_name, not the digest; options.py::_prepare and related.py::contribute_to_class call truncate_name, so they reach the digest transitively.

question: One schema-editor hook exists solely for backends whose requires_literal_defaults feature is on: the base class implementation raises NotImplementedError, and exactly two concrete editors override it with the identical one-line body `return self.quote_value(value)`. Identify the override whose delegate first tries to adapt the value through the standard library's sqlite3 module inside a try block, renders booleans as 0/1, emits byte strings as a hexadecimal literal behind a single X character, and raises ValueError for any other type. Return the qualified symbol as path::name.

evidence.contains: requires_literal_defaults must provide a prepare_default() method
"Cannot quote parameter value %r of type %s" % (value, type(value))

author_notes: Difficulty clauses 4 and 5. Clause 4: prepare_default is defined three times in the corpus (django/db/backends/base/schema.py:411, django/db/backends/oracle/schema.py:200, django/db/backends/sqlite3/schema.py:74), and the two overrides are textually identical - both are exactly 'return self.quote_value(value)'. Reading either override, or all three definitions, cannot decide the question. Clause 5: the described behaviour belongs to the callee, not to the named hook, so the answer is only correct given what quote_value resolves to on each backend. quote_value itself has five definitions (base, mysql, oracle, postgresql, sqlite3); only the SQLite one wraps 'import sqlite3; value = sqlite3.adapt(value)' in a try block, returns str(int(value)) for bools, returns "X'%s'" % value.hex() for bytes, and raises ValueError('Cannot quote parameter value %r of type %s'). So the chain prepare_default -> quote_value must be walked per backend. Proof: sqlite3/schema.py:43-75 contains both definitions; oracle/schema.py:29-41 shows its quote_value formatting dates and durations with duration_iso_string and falling back to str(value) instead of raising. Alternates fail: oracle's override is the namesake whose delegate has none of the described behaviour (no sqlite3 adaptation, no X-prefixed hex, no ValueError); the base definition only raises NotImplementedError and is the symbol a first search surfaces; sqlite3/schema.py::quote_value is the method that actually implements the described behaviour but is not the hook the question asks for (the question asks for the requires_literal_defaults hook); mysql/schema.py::quote_value delegates to the driver's escape() instead; base/schema.py::_column_default_sql is the neighbouring default-related hook and returns a placeholder template.

question: Entering the SQLite schema editor asks the connection to turn foreign key enforcement off and raises NotSupportedError when that call reports a falsy result. Three classes in the corpus define that connection method. Identify the one that can legitimately report failure: it issues its disabling statement and then reads the setting back, because the change is silently ignored in the middle of a multi-statement transaction. Return the qualified symbol as path::name.

evidence.contains: "SQLite schema editor cannot be used while foreign key "
Always return True to indicate constraint checks
Backends can implement as needed to temporarily disable foreign key

author_notes: Difficulty clauses 1, 4 and 5. Clause 4: disable_constraint_checking is defined three times (django/db/backends/base/base.py:540, django/db/backends/mysql/base.py:300, django/db/backends/sqlite3/base.py:244) and only one matches the description. Clause 1: a search for a version that can report failure lands first on the base definition, which does nothing at all and plainly 'return False' - the most plausible early hit, and wrong, because the question requires a definition that issues a disabling statement and then verifies it. MySQL's override is the second plausible hit and its docstring even says 'Always return True to indicate constraint checks need to be re-enabled', which is the opposite of the described behaviour. Clause 5: the described contract only exists because of the caller - sqlite3/schema.py's context entry ('if not self.connection.disable_constraint_checking(): raise NotSupportedError(...)') - so the significance of the return value cannot be read off any single definition; the SQLite override's 'PRAGMA foreign_keys = OFF' followed by re-reading 'PRAGMA foreign_keys' and returning 'not bool(enabled)' is what makes the caller's guard reachable. Proof: sqlite3/base.py:244-250 for the re-read and conditional return; sqlite3/schema.py:25-36 for the guard and the NotSupportedError text. Alternates fail: MySQL's override unconditionally returns True after 'SET foreign_key_checks=0'; the base definition returns False without executing anything, so it never 'issues its disabling statement'; sqlite3's enable_constraint_checking only turns the pragma back on and returns nothing; base/base.py::constraint_checks_disabled is the contextmanager that consumes the return value rather than producing it; sqlite3's check_constraints is the separate PRAGMA foreign_key_check verifier run on exit.

question: In the PostgreSQL schema editor, the ALTER COLUMN ... TYPE template acquires a cast suffix only when one helper returns a non-empty fragment. That helper returns the fragment when the resolved data types of the old and the new field differ, except that when both fields are array fields of the same internal type it instead compares the two sequences of element base data types. Which method makes that decision? Return the qualified symbol as path::name.
author_notes: Difficulty clauses 1, 3 and 5. Clause 1: every phrase in the description that a search can key on ('array field', 'base data types') resolves first to _field_base_data_types, the recursive generator that yields the element types, and to _field_data_type, which resolves one field's type. Both are distractors: they compute the inputs, they do not decide anything. Clause 3: the real path is three hops - the public alter_field/_alter_field flow reaches postgresql/schema.py::_alter_column_type_sql, which sets self.sql_alter_column_type and appends the fragment via the walrus 'if using_sql := self._using_sql(new_field, old_field)', and only that helper contains the branch on array fields versus a plain type comparison. Clause 5: the helper is a two-line-looking predicate whose meaning depends entirely on its callee (_field_base_data_types recursing through base_field for nested ArrayFields) and on its caller (which concatenates the returned fragment onto the mutated sql_alter_column_type template), so no single definition answers the question. Proof: postgresql/schema.py:122-134 for the decision, 164-165 for the consumption, 76-81 for the generator. Alternates fail: _field_base_data_types only yields base types and makes no decision; _field_data_type resolves a single field's database type; postgresql's _alter_column_type_sql consumes the fragment but delegates the decision, and its own distinct behaviour is dropping _like indexes and handling identity columns; base/schema.py::_alter_column_type_sql is the generic namesake with no cast logic at all; oracle's _alter_field_type_workaround is the same-flavoured 'type change needs extra SQL' method on a different backend.

question: The backend-independent connection wrapper declares a hook for detecting rows with invalid foreign key references after enforcement has been switched off, and its own docstring proposes 'SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE' as a way a backend might implement it. Five classes in the corpus define that hook. Enumerate every definition that ignores the table names it is passed and implements exactly that proposal, executing the immediate statement on a cursor and then restoring deferred mode. Return each as path::name in a JSON list.

def check_constraints(self, table_names=None):
        """

        afterward.

author_notes: Difficulty clauses 1, 2 and 4. Clause 4: check_constraints is defined five times - django/db/backends/base/base.py:555, mysql/base.py:323, oracle/base.py:327, postgresql/base.py:476, sqlite3/base.py:257 - and exactly two of them match the description. Clause 1: the first and most quotable hit for 'SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE' is the base class docstring itself, which contains the phrase verbatim while its body is a bare 'pass'; a system that stops at the strongest textual match answers with the base definition, which implements nothing. Clause 2: the answer is a set that must be assembled from two separate definitions in two different backend packages, and each must be checked against the two rejected implementations that do real per-row work, so no single definition suffices. Proof: oracle/base.py:327-335 and postgresql/base.py:476-484 are byte-identical - same docstring, 'SET CONSTRAINTS ALL IMMEDIATE' followed by 'SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED', and table_names is never read. MySQL's version defaults table_names from introspection.table_names and issues a LEFT JOIN per relation to find violating rows; SQLite's runs 'PRAGMA foreign_key_check' and raises IntegrityError per violation; both therefore use the table names and do not implement the proposal. The base definition is a documented no-op. constraint_checks_disabled and disable_constraint_checking are the neighbouring hooks that switch enforcement off rather than verify it.

question: The database-backed cache backend, after deleting rows whose expiry has passed, may still hold more entries than its configured maximum; it then asks the connection's operations object for a parameterized query that returns the first cache key above the n smallest, so that everything ordered below that key can be deleted in one statement. question: Registering a serialization format whose module cannot be imported does not fail at registration time. Instead the registry stores a dynamically constructed module-like type whose two entry-point attributes are the same stub instance, and that instance carries the original import error. The error only resurfaces later, when the stored stub is invoked - either because the format is used to build a serializer instance or because a stream is turned back into objects through the stored entry point. Which method on that stub performs the deferred re-raise? Return the qualified symbol as path::name.
author_notes: Gold is BadSerializer's invocation method (def at django/core/serializers/__init__.py:51), which raises the exception captured at registration. Clause 1: searching for the import-failure behaviour lands on register_serializer, which builds BadSerializer(exc) and the synthetic BadSerializerModule type - that is the registration half and the obvious stopping point, but it never raises; the raise is one step further, in the stub's invocation method. Clause 2: the answer only follows from combining three definitions - register_serializer (stores the stub under both Serializer and Deserializer), the stub class (holds the exception), and the use sites serialize/deserialize, where get_serializer(format)() instantiates the stub and get_deserializer(format) is then called, which is what triggers the stored error. Clause 4: the leaf name is defined 19 times across the corpus, so the question requires path::name. Clause 5: the stub method is meaningless in isolation - whether it ever runs depends entirely on the callers, since a serializer entry point is used by instantiation while a deserializer entry point is used by direct call, and the same stub object serves both. Alternates: register_serializer is the designed trap (it constructs, but does not raise); the stub's initializer only stores the exception; get_serializer/_load_serializers route and populate the registry, raising SerializerDoesNotExist only for unknown formats; SerializerDoesNotExist is that unrelated lookup error class.
